title: Button against the big blind
summary: The most common 6-max spot: who opens what, who defends what and who the flop favors.

why.text: The most common 6-max spot: everyone folds to the button, it opens, the big blind defends. The button has position on every street; the big blind has a discount, it already put in 1 BB.

bb.caption: Big blind against a button open: 3-bet and call.

postflop.text:
After the flop:
- On high dry boards (K♠ 7♦ 2♣, A♥ 8♣ 3♦) the button has the range advantage: small, frequent c-bets.
- On low and middle connected boards (8♠ 7♦ 6♣, 6♥ 5♥ 4♠) the big blind is strong: it has more two pair, sets and straights. The button checks more, the big blind check-raises more.
- Out of position the big blind realizes less equity, so on wet boards it should defend with check-raises too, not only calls.

q-board.q: Flop 6♥ 5♥ 4♠, the button opened and the big blind called. Who has the nut advantage?
q-board.explain: The big blind defends with many low and connected hands (87, 75, 64, 54, small pairs), while much of the button's range is high cards that missed this board.

t1.q: Why does the big blind defend wide against the button?
options: It already put in 1 BB and gets good pot odds
t1.explain: The discount on the call makes many hands profitable to defend.

t2.q: On which flop is a small, frequent c-bet easiest for the button?
t2.explain: A high dry board favors the opener’s range.

t3.q: About how much of the deck does the button open in the simplified range?
t3.explain: Late position and only the blinds behind: almost half of all hands.
